opus-5.5.text:
I actually think they're much more similar than people assume. In both cases you're trying to solve a problem that the world hasn't solved yet, and you need to figure out what the highest-leverage thing you can do is. The core skills are the same: you need to find great people, you need to be relentless about execution, and you need to be honest with yourself about whether what you're doing is actually working.

The big difference is the feedback loop. In a startup, the market tells you pretty quickly whether you're creating value. Customers pay you or they don't. In a charity, the people you're helping usually aren't the ones paying, so you can drift for years doing something that feels good but isn't very effective, and nobody forces you to confront that. So you have to build that discipline yourself. You have to measure impact really rigorously and be willing to kill things that aren't working, even when donors like them.

The other thing is scale and capital. With a startup, if you create a lot of value, you can raise enormous amounts of money and grow very fast. Charities are much more constrained; fundraising doesn't scale with impact in the same clean way. That's partly why I ended up thinking that for some problems, building a company is actually the more impactful path. If you can align making money with doing good, you get the market's feedback and its capital working for you, rather than fighting against gravity the whole time.

But honestly, for me, starting a charity young was an incredible education. It taught me to think about impact per dollar and per hour, and that mindset carries over directly into how I think about building a company now.

fable-5.1.text:
I think they're far more similar than people expect, and the differences are mostly about what you can't do rather than what you want to do.

When I started ClimateScience, I was about seventeen, and I treated it exactly like a startup. You have a problem, you have a hypothesis about how to solve it, you need to find people who believe in it enough to work on it, and you need to figure out distribution. In our case the problem was that climate education was either nonexistent or so dry that nobody engaged with it, and the hypothesis was that if you made it genuinely good and genuinely free, it would spread. That's a product thesis. It's not different in kind from what you'd pitch to a VC.

The big difference is incentives. In a startup you can pay people, and money is a very clean coordination mechanism. In a charity you mostly can't, or not much, so you're recruiting purely on mission. That sounds like a disadvantage, and in some ways it is, because you lose a lot of great people who need a salary. But it also acts as a filter. Everyone who shows up is there because they actually care, and that means you get a kind of intensity you'd struggle to buy. We had hundreds of volunteers across dozens of countries, and nobody was there for the equity.

The other difference is the feedback loop. A startup has revenue, and revenue is brutal but honest. If people don't pay, you're wrong. A charity doesn't get that, so you have to be much more deliberate about building your own measurement. Otherwise you can spend years feeling good about something that isn't working, and the people funding you often won't tell you, because the social dynamics around donations are different from the dynamics around customers.

So the way I'd frame it is: a charity is a startup where you've removed one of the hardest constraints, the need to make money, and in exchange you've removed one of the most useful signals. You have to replace that signal yourself. And the recruiting lesson carried over directly to Magic. If you build something people genuinely want to be part of, the mission does a lot of the work that compensation would otherwise have to do. It's just that in a company, you get to use both.

astra-6.text:
I think they’re more similar than people might assume. In both cases, you’re trying to solve a problem, you need a good team, and you have limited resources. You have to figure out what actually works rather than just what sounds compelling.

The biggest difference is the feedback loop. In a startup, customers paying for your product is at least some evidence that you’re creating something they value. In a charity, the people funding you often aren’t the people you’re helping. So you have to be much more deliberate about measuring whether your work is actually improving people’s lives.

In either case, I’d start with the problem, not with the desire to start an organization. Who’s already working on it? Could you help them do more? Starting something new makes sense when there’s an important gap and you have a credible way to fill it.

sol-6.1.text:
I think the biggest similarity is that you’re trying to solve a problem under uncertainty, with limited resources. You need to find something people actually need, build a team, and learn quickly. Being a charity doesn’t make those things less important.

The big difference is the feedback loop. In a startup, revenue gives you a signal that somebody values what you’re doing. It’s imperfect, but it’s useful. In a charity, the person funding the work often isn’t the person benefiting from it. So you have to be much more deliberate about asking: Are we actually helping? What would have happened without us? And is this the best use of the next dollar?

I’d start with the problem in both cases. Then choose the structure that makes it easiest to solve.
